title: Do You Know That Florence Is Packed with Visitors? Evaluating State-of-the-art Models of Speaker Commitment
research_question: How well do state-of-the-art speaker-commitment models generalize to naturally occurring discourse, and which linguistic constructions systematically explain their errors?
methodology: The authors evaluate existing speaker-commitment systems on CommitmentBank, which contains 1,200 naturally occurring English examples involving complements of clause-embedding verbs under negation, modality, questions, and conditionals, drawn from newswire, fiction, and dialogue. At least eight native-English Mechanical Turk annotators rate the speaker's commitment on a graded scale, and a 556-item high-agreement subset is used for detailed analysis. The study compares a linguistically informed rule-based system with linear, tree, and hybrid biLSTM models trained in a multi-task setting on four existing factuality datasets, using Pearson correlation, mean absolute error, and a three-class commitment analysis. citeturn991644view8turn991644view9

key_findings.finding: The linguistically informed rule-based model outperforms the evaluated biLSTM models on the full CommitmentBank, but all systems perform substantially worse there than on their original reference datasets.

Pearson correlation on the full set is 0.41 for the rule-based model versus 0.24, 0.09, and 0.23 for the linear, tree, and hybrid biLSTMs; on the restricted set the corresponding values are 0.50, 0.31, 0.13, and 0.33.

The rule-based model captures negation relatively well with r=0.45 but performs poorly on modal and question environments, while the hybrid model is more consistent across negation, modality, and questions; both fail on conditionals.
Both models have essentially no useful correlation on neg-raising examples, with r=0.04 for the rule-based model and -0.07 for the hybrid model.
In the three-way classification analysis, neither system reliably recognizes the no-commitment class: its F1 is 0 for the rule-based model and 0.11 for the hybrid model.
The systems are better at recognizing commitment polarity than its graded strength: the rule-based system tends toward extreme predictions while the hybrid model struggles with negative commitment.
Both systems achieve their strongest correlation on dialogue and their weakest correlation on newswire, demonstrating substantial genre sensitivity.

limitations: CommitmentBank is English-only and restricted to complements of clause-embedding verbs in four selected entailment-canceling environments, so it does not cover the full range of discourse revision phenomena. citeturn991644view8
Detailed error analysis focuses on a 556-item high-agreement subset, which intentionally excludes many ambiguous judgments and contains only a subset of the original corpus.

The evaluated systems are transferred from other factuality datasets rather than optimized directly for CommitmentBank, making the experiment primarily a test of linguistic generalization rather than the best achievable in-domain performance. citeturn991644view9

Speaker commitment represents what a speaker presents as true, false, or uncertain; it does not independently establish objective truth, so it cannot by itself distinguish a claimed completion from externally confirmed completion.
The dataset does not explicitly label longitudinal relations such as supersession, correction, supplementation, reopening, or conflict resolution.
raw_claims: CommitmentBank contains 1,200 naturally occurring examples of speaker commitment.
Its examples cover negation, modal, question, and conditional environments.
The corpus includes newswire, fiction, and conversational dialogue.
Speaker commitment is annotated as a graded judgment rather than only a binary truth label.
The rule-based system generalizes better overall than the tested biLSTM systems.
Negation is the strongest environment for the rule-based system.
Both evaluated model families perform poorly on conditional inferences.
Neg-raising is difficult for both systems.
Neither system reliably recognizes cases where the speaker has no clear commitment.
Current models capture commitment polarity better than fine-grained commitment strength.
Performance varies substantially across discourse genres.
